source_refs.note: Exercise 14.2, Question 7: cos(alpha + beta) by the dot product (book p.275), as in Example 8; unit vectors at alpha and -beta. Original figure drawn for the answer.

blocks.explanation:
A trigonometric identity proved with vectors, like Example 8 of the book (which proves \(\cos(\alpha - \beta)\)).
Idea: find the dot product of two unit vectors in two ways, once with the angle and once with components, and compare.
Plan: put one unit vector at angle \(\alpha\) above the x-axis and the other at angle \(\beta\) below it, so the angle between them is \(\alpha + \beta\).
steps:
Given: angles \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).
To prove: \(\cos(\alpha + \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta\).
Method: For unit vectors \(\underline{u}\), \(\underline{v}\): \(\underline{u}\cdot\underline{v} = \cos\theta\) (definition) and \(\underline{u}\cdot\underline{v} = a_1a_2 + b_1b_2\) (components). Equate the two.

Choose the two unit vectors
Let \(\underline{OA}\) make angle \(\alpha\) with the positive x-axis (above it) and \(\underline{OB}\) make angle \(\beta\) below it, both of length 1, in the xy-plane.
\[\angle AOB = \alpha + \beta\]
Why: One angle is measured up and the other down from the x-axis, so together they make \(\alpha + \beta\) (see the figure).

Write them in components
\[\underline{OA} = \cos\alpha\,\underline{i} + \sin\alpha\,\underline{j}\]
\[\underline{OB} = \cos\beta\,\underline{i} - \sin\beta\,\underline{j}\]
Why: A unit vector at angle \(\phi\) is \(\cos\phi\,\underline{i} + \sin\phi\,\underline{j}\). For \(OB\) the angle is \(-\beta\), and \(\cos(-\beta) = \cos\beta\), \(\sin(-\beta) = -\sin\beta\).

Dot product from the definition
\[\underline{OA}\cdot\underline{OB}\]
\[= |\underline{OA}||\underline{OB}|\cos(\alpha + \beta)\]
\[= (1)(1)\cos(\alpha + \beta)\]
\[= \cos(\alpha + \beta)\]
Why: Both are unit vectors and the angle between them is \(\alpha + \beta\).

Dot product from components
\[\underline{OA}\cdot\underline{OB}\]
\[= \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha(-\sin\beta)\]
\[= \cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta\]
Why: Multiply matching components and add.

Compare
\[\cos(\alpha + \beta)\]
\[= \cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta\]
Why: Both expressions are the same dot product.

Check
\[\alpha = \beta = 45^{\circ}:\ \cos 90^{\circ} = 0\]
\[\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\]
\[= \tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{1}{2} = 0 \;\checkmark\]
Why: A quick numerical test agrees with the identity.

answer_figure.alt: Unit circle with centre O. Unit vector OA makes angle alpha above the positive x-axis, at A(cos alpha, sin alpha); unit vector OB makes angle beta below it, at B(cos beta, -sin beta). The angle AOB is alpha + beta.
